Section 01The starting point of the spectroscopy program

This paper develops a way to combine nonadiabatic molecular dynamics with cavity photon loss in calculations of two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy. Its numerical examples focus on monomer and dimer exciton–cavity systems. Those small systems are not merely reduced versions of a large ensemble: they make the optical pathways, anharmonic excitation ladders, and stochastic loss representation visible enough to derive and test explicitly.

The method is called Lindblad–partially linearized density matrix dynamics, or L-PLDM. The molecular environment is treated through forward–backward mapping trajectories and partially linearized nuclear motion. Cavity loss is supplied by an additional dissipative construction. The spectrum requires three optical interactions and propagation through ground, single-excitation, and double-excitation sectors.

These notes work through all of those layers. We first build the actual monomer and dimer matrices. We then derive causal response and a matrix representation of left/right actions, explain the partially linearized estimator, and examine the stochastic amplitude-damping construction on arbitrary complex dyads. Finally we connect the dynamics to optical peaks and coherence measurements.

The attached Python program is a finite-dimensional Lindblad and estimator-validation reference, not an implementation of the full PLDM nuclear dynamics. Its purpose is to provide independently checkable matrix tests for the algebra used in the notes.

Primary source: J. Chem. Phys. 159, 094102 (2023). The repository PDF contains the 16-page article followed by nine pages of supplementary material, beginning at PDF page 17. The full published author list includes Justin Provazza. Tutorial equation numbers are independent of article and supplement numbering.

Section 02The model, the spaces, and the units

For N two-level molecules coupled to one cavity mode and local harmonic environments, write

H=[(⨂n=1NHn)⊗Hc]⊗HB,Hn=span{|gn⟩,|en⟩}.
(1)

The molecular excitation operator is σ^n†=|en⟩⟨gn|, embedded with identities on all other factors. The cavity ladder operator obeys a^|q⟩=q|q−1⟩. A local bath can have many harmonic modes even though the molecular electronic system is two-level.

We use energy-valued couplings vn=ℏgn, molecular energies ϵn, and cavity energy Ec. For a wavenumber ν~ in cm−1, E=hcν~. An angular-frequency bath cutoff corresponding to γ~ has a time scale τ=(2πcγ~)−1. These conversions must not lose the factor 2π.

Useful numerical constants are ℏ=658.2119569 meV·fs and 1 cm−1≈0.1239841984 meV. For example, a cutoff of 18 cm−1 corresponds to approximately 295 fs under the angular-frequency convention, whereas 200 cm−1 corresponds to approximately 26.5 fs.

Section 03Local operators: a two-level molecule is not a harmonic oscillator

In the ordered basis (|g⟩,|e⟩),

[σ^]=(0100),[σ^†]=(0010),[n^]=(0001).
(2)

Direct multiplication gives

σ^2=(σ^†)2=0,[σ^,σ^†]=I^−2n^.
(3)

On different molecules the operators commute. This is often called a hard-core excitation algebra: each molecule can carry zero or one electronic excitation. The photon has no such local saturation in the full Fock space. In the truncated photon basis (|0⟩,|1⟩,|2⟩),

[a^]=(010002000).
(4)

The 2 factor produces a non-equally spaced Jaynes–Cummings ladder when the molecule is two-level. Forgetting that factor destroys the correct ESA transitions even if the first-manifold polariton splitting remains correct.

Section 04The full Hamiltonian and a possible dimer hopping term

An explicit form is

H^= H^S⊗I^B+I^S⊗H^B+∑nn^n⊗B^n,H^S= Eca^†a^+∑nϵnn^n+∑n<m(Jnmσ^n†σ^m+Jnm∗σ^m†σ^n)+∑n(vnσ^n†a^+vn∗a^†σ^n).
(5)

The direct excitonic coupling Jnm is relevant to a coupled molecular dimer. It is distinct from the cavity-mediated hybridization, and it is absent in the simplest noninteracting molecular ensemble used in the later collective papers.

The bath terms are

H^B=∑nα(P^nα22mnα+12mnαωnα2R^nα2),B^n=∑αcnαR^nα.
(6)

At a specified bath configuration, the matrix diagonal uses ϵn+∑αcnαRnα. A reorganization counterterm must be handled consistently with whether ϵn is a vertical or minimum-to-minimum energy. The spectral-density convention should be specified before using quoted reorganization energies.

Source: model and response definitions, the later model sections, and the dimer supplement. Complex couplings and explicit tensor-product identities are tutorial notation.

Section 05The monomer has five states through two excitations

For one molecule, use

Bmono=(|G⟩,|c⟩,|e⟩,|cc⟩,|ce⟩)=(|g,0⟩,|g,1⟩,|e,0⟩,|g,2⟩,|e,1⟩).
(7)

The Hamiltonian is

[H^S]Bmono=(000000Ecv∗000vϵ000002Ec2v∗0002vEc+ϵ).
(8)

The molecular population and photon number matrices are

[n^e]=diag(0,0,1,0,1),[n^c]=diag(0,1,0,2,1).
(9)

The raising part of the molecular dipole and the photon annihilation operator are

μ^+=d(|e⟩⟨G|+|ce⟩⟨c|),a^=|G⟩⟨c|+2|c⟩⟨cc|+|e⟩⟨ce|.
(10)

There is no |e,0⟩→|e,e⟩ transition: there is only one molecule. ESA is still possible because the first polariton includes a photon component that the molecular dipole can convert into |e,1⟩.

Section 06Diagonalizing the resonant monomer

Choose real positive v and resonance Ec=ϵ. In the first manifold,

|+⟩=|c⟩+|e⟩2,|−⟩=|c⟩−|e⟩2,E1,±=ϵ±v.
(11)

In the second manifold,

|2,+⟩=|cc⟩+|ce⟩2,|2,−⟩=|cc⟩−|ce⟩2,E2,±=2ϵ±2v.
(12)

The ground-to-first transition amplitudes are ⟨+|μ^+|G⟩=d/2 and ⟨−|μ^+|G⟩=−d/2 for this phase convention. The second-manifold transition amplitudes follow by applying μ^+ to the photon part of each first-manifold state.

For example,

⟨2,+|μ^+|+⟩=d/2,E2,+−E1,+=ϵ+(2−1)v.
(13)

The transition energy is different from E1,+−EG=ϵ+v. This elementary anharmonicity explains why the negative ESA structure does not sit exactly on the positive fundamental feature in a monomer spectrum.

Section 07The bath projector in the polariton basis

The local molecular population is positive and diagonal in (|c⟩,|e⟩). Transform with

[U^]=12(111−1),[n^e](+,−)=U^†(0001)U^=12(1−1−11).
(14)

Both diagonal entries are +1/2. They are molecular probabilities and cannot become negative. Changing the phase of |−⟩ flips the off-diagonal signs but does not change the positive diagonals.

The bath therefore creates both diagonal fluctuations and transitions between the two polaritons. Reducing diagonal displacement is not equivalent to deleting the off-diagonal bath matrix element. For a uniform ensemble, additional bright–dark matrix elements further complicate this distinction.

If a two-state effective Hamiltonian is written with σ^z, remember that n^e=(I^−σ^z)/2 or (I^+σ^z)/2 depending on the chosen basis convention. Dropping the identity contribution is sometimes harmless for unitary system dynamics but can obscure the origin of bath energy shifts. Always reconstruct the original projector as a check.

Section 08A complete eight-state dimer matrix

For two molecules, the ordered basis is

Bdimer=(|G⟩;|c⟩,|1⟩,|2⟩;|cc⟩,|c1⟩,|c2⟩,|12⟩).
(15)

Take J12=J real for clarity. Then

[H^1]=(Ecv1∗v2∗v1ϵ1Jv2Jϵ2),
(16)
[H^2]=(2Ec2v1∗2v2∗02v1Ec+ϵ1Jv2∗2v2JEc+ϵ2v1∗0v2v1ϵ1+ϵ2).
(17)

Direct hopping connects |c1⟩ and |c2⟩, but it cannot move an excitation in |12⟩ onto an already excited molecule. A biexciton interaction would add a separate energy shift to |12⟩; it is not generated automatically by a two-level local basis.

The bath projectors are diag(0;0,1,0;0,1,0,1) and diag(0;0,0,1;0,0,1,1). The molecular raising-dipole block from the first to the second manifold is

[μ^+]21=(000d100d2000d2d1).
(18)

These matrices are sufficient to construct every ground-state third-order pathway for the finite dimer cutoff. The code constructs the same operators from occupation labels, providing an independent check on the displayed blocks.

Section 09Bright and dark dimer combinations

For identical molecules and equal real cavity couplings, define

|B⟩=|1⟩+|2⟩2,|D⟩=|1⟩−|2⟩2.
(19)

In (|c⟩,|B⟩,|D⟩), the first-manifold Hamiltonian is

[H^1]=(Ec2v02vϵ+J000ϵ−J).
(20)

The dark eigenstate has energy ϵ−J, while the bright state hybridizes with the photon. With equal dipoles, ⟨D|μ^+|G⟩=0. With unequal dipoles it becomes (d1−d2)/2; “dark” with respect to the cavity and “dark” with respect to a particular optical polarization need not coincide.

The bath Hamiltonian restricted to the molecular bright/dark pair is

[H^SBint](B,D)=12(B^1+B^2B^1−B^2B^1−B^2B^1+B^2).
(21)

The bath difference drives bright–dark mixing. If the baths were identical operators rather than statistically identical independent baths, that difference would vanish. This makes the locality assumption physically consequential even for just two molecules.

Section 10Using the supplementary matrices responsibly

The appended supplement develops dimer energy-level and dipole information and displays additional pathway-resolved spectra. It is particularly useful for connecting transitions in the second manifold to signed structures in the two-dimensional map.

A table of rounded eigenvectors should not be used as the numerical transformation matrix in a propagation code. Recompute eigenvectors from the specified Hamiltonian, then verify U^†U^=I^, U^†H^U^=diag(Ea), and the transformed dipole. Near degeneracies, even small rounding changes can obscure orthogonality, while an eigenvector's global phase changes dipole signs but not complete physical products.

The symbolic dimer above is intentionally a transparent teaching case. The article's asymmetric parameter sets and the supplementary printed matrices should be reconstructed from their own parameters before quantitative comparison. The tutorial does not substitute newly chosen symmetric parameters for the published dimer and call the result a reproduction.

Supplement guide: energy-level construction, tabulated eigenstates, dipole matrices, and additional spectra and assignments.

Section 11Deriving the optical response from the density equation

Let the applied field interact through V^(t)=−E(t)μ^. In the interaction picture,

∂tρ^I(t)=iℏE(t)[μ^I(t),ρ^I(t)].
(22)

The integral equation is

ρ^I(t)=ρ^eq+iℏ∫−∞tdsE(s)[μ^I(s),ρ^I(s)].
(23)

Substituting this expression twice into its own right-hand side gives the third-order term. With ordered interactions separated by t1,t2,t3, the impulse response can be written

R(3)(t3,t2,t1)=(iℏ)3Tr[μ^G^(t3)μ^×G^(t2)μ^×G^(t1)μ^×ρ^eq].
(24)

Here μ^×O^=[μ^,O^]. The detection interval is t3, the waiting interval is t2, and the first coherence interval is t1. The propagator is defined on the complete space needed to carry the environment's memory. In a finite bath-free Lindblad reference it is a system-space semigroup; in an exact non-Markovian derivation it is the full system–bath propagator.

The third-order response is linear in the prepared initial operator, but a selected pathway is not necessarily a physical density operator. Its trace and positivity are not normalization constraints to enforce during propagation.

Section 12An explicit Liouville-space representation

Choose column vectorization, so for a two-state system

|ρ^⟩⟩=(ρgg,ρeg,ρge,ρee)T.
(25)

The identity

|A^O^B^⟩⟩=(B^T⊗A^)|O^⟩⟩
(26)

gives left/right dipole matrices and the Hamiltonian generator:

[μ^L]=I^⊗μ^,[μ^R]=μ^T⊗I^,[K^H]=−iℏ(I^⊗H^−H^T⊗I^).
(27)

For μ^=d(|e⟩⟨g|+|g⟩⟨e|), the commutator matrix is

[μ^×]=d(01−10100−1−10010−110).
(28)

Acting on (1,0,0,0)T gives d(0,1,−1,0)T, corresponding to d|e⟩⟨g|−d|g⟩⟨e|. This is the first optical commutator, with both ket and bra coherences and their relative sign visible.

For the monomer and dimer cutoffs, the Liouville dimensions are 25 and 64. These are convenient reference sizes even though the production trajectory method uses a different representation.

Section 13Following a rephasing GSB pathway

Let L±O^=μ^±O^ and R±O^=O^μ^±. A rephasing ground-state-bleach pathway begins with R−, then R+, then L+:

|G⟩⟨G|⟶|G⟩⟨e|⟶|G⟩⟨G|⟶|e′⟩⟨G|.
(29)

The first optical coherence evolves with e+i(Ee−EG)t1/ℏ; the last evolves with e−i(Ee′−EG)t3/ℏ. In the simplest one-transition model, the intermediate ground population has no electronic waiting phase.

A non-Markovian bath can still remember the first interval. The operator returned to the ground electronic sector need not carry the equilibrium ground-state bath. Replacing it by a fresh thermal bath would erase part of the echo and spectral-diffusion physics.

The name “bleach” describes the response contribution to absorption relative to the unperturbed sample. It is not an instruction to subtract an arbitrary population from a plotted spectrum after propagation.

Section 14Stimulated emission and excited-state absorption

The rephasing stimulated-emission sequence is R−,L+,R+, while ESA is R−,L+,L+:

SE:|G⟩⟨e|→|e′⟩⟨e|→|e′⟩⟨G|,ESA:|G⟩⟨e|→|e′⟩⟨e|→|f⟩⟨e|,|f⟩∈H2.
(30)

Both can carry a waiting-time coherence |e′⟩⟨e|, but they detect different transitions. The ESA frequency is (Ef−Ee)/ℏ, not (Ee′−EG)/ℏ.

With a common global phase stripped from the response, GSB and SE have positive relative sign and ESA negative. The corresponding nonrephasing sequences are L+,L−,L+, L+,R−,R+, and L+,R−,L+. Detect every final branch with Tr(μ^−O^).

This table is a complete recipe for the usual six selected ground-state RWA pathways, not a replacement for the eight unselected terms obtained by expanding three commutators. The selection depends on phase matching and the positive/negative optical frequencies retained.

Section 15Fourier signs and the meaning of an absorptive spectrum

For rephasing, use e−iω1t1+iω3t3; for nonrephasing, use e+iω1t1+iω3t3. These choices place positive excitation energies on the same displayed first axis despite opposite initial coherence phases.

S~R/NR(ω3,t2,ω1)=∫0∞dt1∫0∞dt3eiω3t3∓iω1t1SR/NR(t3,t2,t1).
(31)

Our phase-stripped convention takes Re(S~R+S~NR). The paper's negative-imaginary-part convention is equivalent when its retained global response factor is restored: if R=−iS, then −ImR=ReS.

A finite propagation window convolves each frequency feature with a numerical line shape. A smoothing function reduces ringing but broadens peaks. Zero-padding makes a denser frequency grid, not a longer physical coherence trace. To resolve a smaller energy separation, increase the available propagation time rather than only the number of zeros appended before an FFT.

Source: Sec. II A and the absorptive convention and smoothing function.

Section 16Why a molecular bath cannot always be replaced by a decay rate

For Gaussian diagonal energy fluctuations, a simple coherence can be expressed through a line-broadening function,

g(t)=1ℏ2∫0tds∫0sduC(u),C(t)=⟨B^(t)B^(0)⟩B.
(32)

A single Markovian pure-dephasing rate replaces this history-dependent structure by a linear-in-time real part of g(t). That may be justified for a fast weak bath, but it loses slow frequency memory and vibronic structure when those are important.

For static Gaussian disorder, the rephasing phase average is exp⁡[−σ2(t3−t1)2/(2ℏ2)], whereas the nonrephasing average contains (t3+t1)2. For a dynamical bath, correlations across all response intervals control how much refocusing survives. A response calculation that draws an independent bath after every pulse cannot reproduce the same memory.

This is part of the motivation for using trajectory-based nonadiabatic dynamics alongside a separate Markovian description of photon leakage: the molecular bath and the external electromagnetic reservoir need not live on the same time scale or justify the same approximation.

Section 17From forward and backward nuclear paths to partial linearization

The density matrix contains one forward quantum amplitude and one backward conjugate amplitude. A nuclear path-integral representation therefore has paths |RF(t)⟩ and |RB(t)⟩. Define their mean and difference,

|R¯⟩=|RF⟩+|RB⟩2,|Z⟩=|RF⟩−|RB⟩.
(33)

For one mass-weighted coordinate, the kinetic-action difference is ∫dtR¯˙Z˙. Integrating by parts moves the time derivative to R¯, leaving a boundary term and −∫dtR¯¨Z. The boundary term combines with the initial density kernel to produce a Wigner transform.

For forward and backward mapped potentials VF and VB, expand

VF(R¯+Z/2)−VB(R¯−Z/2)=VF(R¯)−VB(R¯)+Z2[∂RVF(R¯)+∂RVB(R¯)]+O(Z2).
(34)

Keeping terms only through first order in the difference coordinate makes its path integral impose

R¯¨=−12(∂RVF+∂RVB).
(35)

For ordinary coordinates restore the mass factor. The electronic forward and backward variables remain distinct, and their phases and weights survive. The discarded higher powers of Z are the approximation. The construction is not simply Ehrenfest dynamics applied to a physical density matrix averaged at the beginning.

Source: Sec. II B. The explicit mean/difference expansion here supplies intermediate steps behind the paper's trajectory equations.

Section 18Mapping a finite-state system into oscillator coordinates

The Meyer–Miller–Stock–Thoss mapping associates a basis state |a⟩ with a singly excited mapping oscillator state. On the physical singly excited subspace,

|a⟩⟨b| ⟷ m^a†m^b,m^a=x^a+ip^a2.
(36)

The Weyl symbol of the mapped electronic Hamiltonian has the familiar form, for a real symmetric matrix Vab(R),

Hmap(R,P,x,p)=HB(R,P)+12∑abVab(R)(xaxb+papb−δab).
(37)

The diagonal subtraction is a mapping zero-point term, not a physical cavity vacuum energy. Different mapping estimators and focusing conventions sometimes rearrange this term. Its nuclear derivative must remain consistent with the chosen formulation. Dropping it while retaining an estimator derived with it is not merely a notation change.

Hamilton's equations for mapping coordinates give

x˙a=1ℏ∑bVabpb,p˙a=−1ℏ∑bVabxb.
(38)

With ca=(xa+ipa)/2, these become iℏ|c⟩˙=V^(R)|c⟩. The matrix Schrödinger equation therefore appears naturally within the mapping dynamics. The mapping amplitudes are integration variables with weights; their norm need not be one on every sampled trajectory.

Section 19An explicit Gaussian forward–backward estimator

A useful way to see the electronic algebra is to sample independent complex Gaussian kets |cF⟩ and |cB⟩, each with zero mean and covariance E[cacb∗]=δab. For a given initial matrix ρ^0, assign

W0=⟨cF|ρ^0|cB⟩.
(39)

Then at the initial time,

E[W0|cF⟩⟨cB|]=ρ^0.
(40)

To verify element ab, expand W0=∑ijciF∗(ρ0)ijcjB. Independence yields E[caFciF∗]E[cjBcbB∗]=δaiδjb, leaving (ρ0)ab.

For a prescribed Hamiltonian independent of the sampled amplitudes, both kets propagate with the same unitary U^(t), and the estimator remains exact:

E[W0|cF(t)⟩⟨cB(t)|]=U^(t)ρ^0U^†(t).
(41)

In PLDM the nuclear trajectory depends on the forward and backward mapping variables. That makes the propagation correlated with the sampled estimator and introduces the partially linearized dynamics. The Gaussian identity explains the initial electronic representation but is not by itself a proof of exact system–bath evolution.

Section 20Focused initial conditions and their limits

For a simple basis dyad |i⟩⟨j|, a focused electronic initialization uses forward and backward amplitudes concentrated on those labels. This can reduce the variance associated with Gaussian mapping sampling. Optical interactions create superpositions; those can be decomposed or importance sampled into new focused dyads.

However, a representation identity at one instant does not mean every alternative amplitude distribution produces the same approximate nuclear dynamics. If the trajectory force is nonlinear in the sampled amplitudes, changing the distribution can change the approximation as well as its variance. A focusing prescription should be tied to the estimator and approximation used in the method.

For a branch W|f⟩⟨b|, an observable is evaluated as

Tr(A^W|f⟩⟨b|)=W⟨b|A^|f⟩.
(42)

No dense density matrix need be formed. The later 2025 nonlinear paper exploits this rank-one structure to make optical reinitialization and measurement substantially cheaper. Its detailed sampling derivation is linked at the end of these notes.

Section 21Nuclear forces and thermal initialization

The partially linearized force is the mean of forward and backward mapped forces,

R˙nα=Pnα/mnα,P˙nα=−12∂Rnα[Hmmap(R,P,xF,pF)+Hmmap(R,P,xB,pB)].
(43)

For the diagonal bath coupling, this is a harmonic restoring force plus a contribution from the two mapping population functions. The photon component exerts no direct local molecular displacement force, but light–matter hybridization changes the molecular components that do.

A harmonic bath initially thermal on its ground electronic surface has Wigner variances

⟨Rnα2⟩W=ℏ2mnαωnαcoth⁡βℏωnα2,⟨Pnα2⟩W=mnαℏωnα2coth⁡βℏωnα2.
(44)

The initial positions and momenta are sampled once for the branch history. Subsequent optical interactions change electronic variables and forces, not the fact that the bath carries prior history. Ground-state bleach, stimulated emission, and ESA therefore need their own consistently propagated forward–backward paths.

Section 22Deriving the elementary amplitude-damping master equation

Before combining loss with PLDM, consider a two-state decay |1⟩→|0⟩. Let H^=ℏω|1⟩⟨1| and L^=|0⟩⟨1|. With population-decay rate κ,

ρ^˙=−iℏ[H^,ρ^]+κ(L^ρ^L^†−12{L^†L^,ρ^}).
(45)

Since L^†L^=|1⟩⟨1|, direct matrix multiplication gives

ρ˙11=−κρ11,ρ˙00=κρ11,ρ˙10=(−iω−κ/2)ρ10,ρ˙01=(iω−κ/2)ρ01.
(46)

In column-vectorized order (00,10,01,11), the generator is

[K^]=(000κ0−iω−κ/20000iω−κ/20000−κ).
(47)

The left trace vector is ⟨⟨I|=(1,0,0,1), and ⟨⟨I|K^=0. This checks trace preservation independently of any chosen initial state.

Section 23The exact finite-time loss map

For a loss-only step of length Δt, define η=e−κΔt. The solution is

ρ11′=ηρ11,ρ00′=ρ00+(1−η)ρ11,ρ01′=ηρ01,ρ10′=ηρ10.
(48)

One Kraus representation is

M^0=|0⟩⟨0|+η|1⟩⟨1|,M^1=1−η|0⟩⟨1|,
(49)
ρ^′=M^0ρ^M^0†+M^1ρ^M^1†,M^0†M^0+M^1†M^1=I^.
(50)

For spectator states, M^0 acts as the identity on them and M^1 vanishes. This map is linear and valid on arbitrary operators, not only positive density matrices. That last property matters for spectroscopy, where an optical branch can be a non-Hermitian dyad.

The population decay is η; the coherence decay is η. Applying the population factor to all amplitudes would double the intended population decay rate.

Section 24The paper's stochastic multiplicative construction

Suppose a response operator is represented by ρ^=|f⟩⟨b|, with ρij=fibj∗. The article constructs stochastic amplitude factors whose averaged products generate the desired dissipative map. For the two-state loss channel, define a real random variable s with E[s]=0 and E[s2]=1. A uniform choice is s=3(2r−1), with r uniform on [0,1].

For ρ00≠0, set

q=(1−η)ρ11ρ00,f0′=f0(1+sq),b0′=b0(1+sq∗),
(51)
f1′=ηf1,b1′=ηb1.
(52)

Because b0′∗=b0∗(1+sq), the ground population estimator is ρ00(1+sq)2, not ρ00|1+sq|2. Averaging gives

E[ρ00′]=ρ00(1+q2)=ρ00+(1−η)ρ11.
(53)

The optical coherences have only one ground multiplier, whose mean is one, and therefore acquire the required η factor. The excited population acquires η. This verifies the loss map at the estimator level.

For arbitrary response dyads, q can be complex. Conjugating the wrong multiplier turns q2 into |q|2 and no longer reproduces the desired map. A complex response estimator should not be forced into a positive-probability interpretation.

Source: Sec. II C and the article's stochastic-loss appendix. The derivation here states the conjugation convention explicitly and checks the required moments.

Section 25The singular case and a nonsingular reference estimator

The multiplicative ratio is undefined when ρ00=0. This is a real algebraic limitation of that particular parameterization, not a failure of amplitude damping. A pure excited-state initial condition is a simple example: the exact map creates ground-state population even though multiplying an initially zero ground amplitude by a finite number cannot do so.

An alternative reference construction uses the Kraus sum directly. Choose one Kraus index J with any fixed positive probabilities pJ, and update

|f′⟩=M^J|f⟩pJ,|b′⟩=M^J|b⟩pJ.
(54)

Then

E[|f′⟩⟨b′|]=∑JM^J|f⟩⟨b|M^J†.
(55)

For two channels, p0=p1=1/2 is sufficient for correctness, though not necessarily efficient. This estimator remains valid for zero incoming ground amplitude and for arbitrary complex dyads. It need not preserve trace on each sampled branch, but the average does. It is a tutorial reference, not a claim that the published implementation used this alternative.

Adding a small denominator by hand to the multiplicative method changes its expectation unless a limiting prescription and error analysis are supplied. The reference code therefore tests the nonsingular Kraus identity exactly and uses the multiplicative identity only where its ratio is defined.

Section 26One cavity jump versus several resolved transition jumps

The physical cavity lowering operator within the retained dimer basis is

a^=|G⟩⟨c|+2|c⟩⟨cc|+|1⟩⟨c1|+|2⟩⟨c2|.
(56)

The article describes treating the constituent transition channels independently in its loss construction. A single dissipator κD[a^] and a sum of dissipators for those separately resolved transitions have the same photon-number anticommutator here, but not generally the same recycling term.

For example, take O^=|c1⟩⟨c2|. A collective cavity jump gives

a^O^a^†=|1⟩⟨2|.
(57)

Separate channels |1⟩⟨c1| and |2⟩⟨c2| give zero when each channel acts on both sides of this off-diagonal dyad. The collective channel preserves a coherence in the emitted-photon-unresolved description; independent resolved channels discard that particular cross-channel coherence.

This does not imply that every observable in the two models differs by a large amount. It does mean that a numerical comparison must specify which loss model is used, especially in the two-excitation manifold and in optical coherences. The teaching script tests the distinction explicitly rather than labeling the two constructions identical.

Section 27Combining loss and coherent propagation

Let K^H be the coherent generator at a fixed bath configuration and D^ the loss generator. In general they do not commute. A symmetric split step is

e(K^H+D^)Δt=eD^Δt/2eK^HΔteD^Δt/2+O(Δt3)
(58)

for a local step with suitably regular time-independent generators. The global error over a fixed total interval is second order under the usual stability assumptions. Nuclear timestepping introduces another numerical approximation when the Hamiltonian changes in time.

An exact elementary damping map does not make the combined split propagation exact. The timestep must be converged against the noncommuting light–matter evolution and the changing nuclear forces. Similarly, a stochastic map that has the right first two random moments must still be sampled well enough for the observable of interest.

The small finite-system reference can exponentiate the complete Liouvillian directly. That makes it a useful benchmark for a split or sampled implementation before coupling the method to a large bath.

Section 28Polariton poles in a lossy two-state linear model

For a simple linear-response model, use the non-Hermitian first-manifold matrix

[H^eff]=(Ec−iΓc/2vvϵ−iΓe/2).
(59)

Here Γc and Γe are energy linewidth parameters in the explicitly stated amplitude matrix. At resonance, the poles are

Epole,±=ϵ−i4(Γc+Γe)±v2−(Γc−Γe)216.
(60)

When v>|Γc−Γe|/4, the square root is real and the poles have separated real parts. This pole condition is not by itself a sufficient condition for two visibly resolved peaks in every measured spectrum. Oscillator strengths, overlapping widths, and the detection channel also matter.

This model is useful for checking linewidth factors and limiting cases. It does not replace the molecular non-Markovian bath in the paper, nor does it include recycling into lower response blocks after the second or third optical interaction.

Section 29Reading a polariton coherence time correctly

An isolated upper–lower coherence evolves as

ρ+−(t)=ρ+−(0)e−i(E+−E−)t/ℏe−γ+−t
(61)

when a single exponential decay approximation applies. Its beat period is

Tbeat=2πℏE+−E−.
(62)

The real part of a cross-peak contribution may therefore look like a damped cosine, but the measured intensity usually combines multiple pathways. A fit of the total peak to Ae−t/τcos⁡(Ωt+ϕ)+B(t) needs a justified background B(t), a stable spectral extraction window, and a clear distinction between field amplitude and intensity.

A polariton population lifetime is not the same object as an upper–lower coherence time. Even for simple Markovian decay, coherence damping contains half the sum of the participating population decay rates plus any additional dephasing. Bath-induced transitions to dark states and vibronic coherences add further structure.

The paper's long-lived oscillatory features are predictions within its model and approximation. They motivate experimental tests; they are not evidence that the corresponding experimental coherence was measured in this theoretical study.

Section 30Why diagonal decoupling is not the whole bath problem

For a normalized polariton whose molecular coefficient on each of N identical sites is X/N, a diagonal local fluctuation is

B^PP=|X|2N∑nB^n.
(63)

With independent identical baths, its correlation function is |X|4C(t)/N, and its diagonal reorganization energy is

λP,diag=|X|4Nλ.
(64)

At resonance |X|2=1/2, giving λ/(4N). This is a statement about the diagonal fluctuation projected onto one delocalized state. Off-diagonal coupling to other polaritons or dark states remains. Summing over many dark final states can compensate a small individual matrix element.

For a monomer, there is no extensive dark reservoir, but the off-diagonal polariton bath matrix derived earlier is nonzero. Thus even the smallest example already warns against interpreting a reduced displacement as complete immunity to the molecular environment.

Section 31Interpreting the monomer and dimer spectra

The monomer results let one compare GSB, SE, and ESA as cavity coupling and loss are varied. Positive diagonal and cross-peak structures cannot be interpreted without the negative second-manifold contribution nearby. The excitation ladder supplies the transition energies; the bath and loss determine broadening and waiting-time changes.

The dimer introduces excitonic mixing, additional states in both excitation manifolds, and more possible dipole products. A peak assignment requires the initial coherence energy, the final detection transition, and the intermediate operator during t2. Assigning every plotted coordinate to a single eigenvalue is insufficient for ESA.

The notes and embedded checks preserve these distinctions. They do not infer missing numerical settings from a plotted curve or treat a small bath-free matrix as the published simulation.

Section 32A monomer scale and pole calculator

This calculator reports the monomer's first- and second-manifold energies, ideal beat period, and lossy linear poles. The coupling input is a spectroscopic wavenumber and the loss input is an energy width; the conversion is performed explicitly. The model is resonant and has no molecular bath beyond the optional phenomenological emitter linewidth.

At the default coupling of 500 cm−1, the ideal Rabi splitting is 1000 cm−1, or about 123.984 meV. Its beat period is approximately 33.36 fs. A 10 meV cavity population width corresponds to 65.82 fs for the isolated photon population; it is not automatically the same as the fitted polariton cross-peak coherence time.

Section 33The teaching tests and their scope

The embedded Python program constructs monomer and dimer matrices in occupation bases, checks their excitation blocks and dipoles, verifies the amplitude-damping map on arbitrary complex dyads, and compares collective and independently resolved photon jumps. It also evaluates the Gaussian forward–backward representation for prescribed unitary evolution and provides a lossy monomer spectrum as a small reference example.

python lpldm_foundations_teaching.py --test
python lpldm_foundations_teaching.py --demo --output monomer_reference.csv

The stochastic demonstration has finite-sample error; the exact Kraus and matrix identities are tested by algebraic enumeration. The code does not propagate PLDM nuclear paths and must not be used to label a bath-free curve as an L-PLDM reproduction. Its test names and printed output distinguish exact matrix checks from sampling convergence.

Section 34Twelve worked checks

1. Count the monomer states correctly.
There is one ground state, two first-manifold states, and two second-manifold states. The total is five. The second manifold is (|g,2⟩,|e,1⟩), not a second electronic excitation on the same molecule. A four-state truncation omitting either of these changes ESA.
2. Derive the monomer second-manifold coupling.
Apply vσ^†a^ to |g,2⟩. The photon operator gives 2|g,1⟩, and the molecular operator gives |e,1⟩. Hence the matrix element is 2v, producing eigenvalue shifts ±2v at resonance.
3. Check positivity of the transformed molecular projector.
The matrix 12(1−1−11) has eigenvalues zero and one. It is a projector, since its square equals itself. Its diagonal entries are both 1/2. A matrix with one negative diagonal element cannot represent the same population operator in an orthonormal basis.
4. Verify trace preservation of the elementary loss generator.
Adding the two population equations gives ρ˙00+ρ˙11=κρ11−κρ11=0. In Liouville form the trace row (1,0,0,1) annihilates the generator from the left. This identity holds for arbitrary input operators, not just normalized populations.
5. Apply a finite loss step to a pure excited state.
For ρ^=|1⟩⟨1|, the Kraus sum gives η|1⟩⟨1|+(1−η)|0⟩⟨0|. The multiplicative ground-amplitude ratio is singular because ρ00=0, but the physical map is perfectly well defined. This is why a nonsingular reference map is valuable.
6. Verify the stochastic ground-state population gain.
The random factor product is (1+sq)2=1+2sq+s2q2. Its mean is 1+q2. Multiplying by ρ00 yields ρ00+(1−η)ρ11. Replacing the square by an absolute square would instead insert |q|2 and fail for general complex response operators.
7. Compare collective and resolved jumps on one dimer coherence.
The collective operator maps |c1⟩⟨c2| to |1⟩⟨2| in its recycling term. Each resolved transition acts nontrivially on only one side of that dyad, so its own two-sided recycling contribution is zero. The two generators differ on this coherence even though their photon-number decay terms agree.
8. Find the bare dimer dark energy.
For equal molecular energies ϵ and real hopping J, applying the exciton matrix to (|1⟩−|2⟩)/2 gives (ϵ−J)|D⟩. Equal cavity couplings cancel on this combination. Equal optical dipoles also cancel, but unequal dipoles can make it optically visible.
9. Verify the Gaussian estimator at the initial time.
Expand the weight ∑ijciF∗ρijcjB and multiply by caFcbB∗. The forward and backward averages factorize into δaiδjb. Summing the indices leaves ρab. This proves the electronic representation, not the exactness of the amplitude-dependent nuclear trajectory.
10. Convert a Rabi splitting into a beat period.
For a splitting of 100 meV, T=2πℏ/ΔE=2π(658.2119569)/100≈41.36 fs. Using ℏ/ΔE alone gives the inverse angular frequency, not a full oscillation period.
11. Explain why a response branch should not be normalized to unit trace.
After the first pulse, a branch can be |e⟩⟨G|, whose trace is zero. It carries an optical coherence that is essential to the response. Trace normalization is undefined for this branch and would destroy the perturbative construction. Only the appropriate ensemble of physical density operators must preserve the physical normalization.
12. List the independent convergence tests in a full L-PLDM spectrum.
Converge the nuclear bath discretization, timestep, electronic propagator error, stochastic and mapping trajectory counts, optical delay windows, and Fourier grid/windowing. Check loss-channel definitions and excitation cutoff separately. Small variance or a trace-conserving finite-system map cannot establish accuracy of the partially linearized nuclear approximation.

Section 35A practical route from this paper to the later work

Read this page for the operator and response foundations, then use the 2025 linear-spectroscopy notes to understand how the Hamiltonian and propagator are reorganized for many molecules. Continue to the 2025 nonlinear-spectroscopy notes for explicit importance sampling and branch batching. The PNAS notes then emphasize the physical interpretation of coherence and polaron-decoupling signatures.

The small monomer and dimer are useful throughout this sequence. A method intended for a huge ensemble should first reproduce the simple matrices, finite loss maps, and optical-pathway signs derived here. Those checks are inexpensive, explicit, and much more informative than trusting a complicated spectrum because it looks plausible.
